title: Ha'azinu: give ear, O heavens (Deuteronomy 32:1)
hook: Moses' last song calls heaven and earth as witnesses

segments.voice: Yesterday, hester panim, the hidden face. Your line was hidden, not gone. Did the word hidden change anything? Today, Moses stops speaking and starts to sing. Day five hundred twenty-seven.

Open a Torah scroll almost anywhere and you see columns of text running edge to edge, like the pages of a book. Then you reach Ha'azinu, and the page changes shape. The words split into two narrow columns with a gap down the middle, line answering line. Scribes still copy it that way today. Even someone who can't read a word of Hebrew can see that something different is happening. These words of Moses aren't a speech. They're a song.
screen: `COLUMNS, EDGE TO EDGE.` → `THEN, A PAGE IN TWO.` → `NOT A SPEECH: A SONG.`

segments.voice: It begins: "Give ear, ye heavens, and I will speak; And let the earth hear the words of my mouth." Ha'azinu means give ear: listen closely. In Nitzavim, Moses had called heaven and earth as witnesses. Now he speaks to them directly. Why the sky and the ground? Rashi gives two reasons. First, they last. Moses is mortal, and so is everyone listening, but heaven and earth will still be there to testify long after. Second, they respond. If the people keep the covenant, the heavens give rain and the earth gives its crops; if not, they hold back. Witnesses that can act. There's a playful midrash in the Sifrei too. Moses says give ear to the heavens, the word for listening up close, and only hear to the earth, the word for listening from further off, because he was near to heaven and far from earth. The prophet Isaiah, the midrash notes, says it the other way round: hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth. He was nearer the earth. Under the play is a real point: where you stand shapes how you speak. The song itself is long and fierce, a retelling of the people's story, its gifts and its failures. It's read in synagogue in the fall, around the High Holy Days. And it opens by calling the whole world to listen: the sky above, the ground below, and everyone in between.
screen: `HA'AZINU: GIVE EAR.` · `WITNESSES THAT LAST.` · `WITNESSES THAT RESPOND.` · `ISAIAH SAYS IT THE OTHER WAY.` · then, large: `HEAVEN AND EARTH LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at sky and earth. If you can, go to a window or step outside. If not, picture them. Look up first: the sky, whatever it's doing right now, cloud or blue or dark. Then look down: the ground, the floor, grass, pavement. Moses called these two to listen because they last. Let yourself be small between them for a moment. Breathe in the space between above and below. The bell holds the time.
Ha'azinu. Give ear. The first word of Moses' last song, spoken to the sky.
Your line: heaven and earth listen. Today, look up once and down once, on purpose, and remember who Moses called to listen. Day five hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Ha'azinu is read in synagogue in the fall, usually on the Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur or just after; in the Torah scroll it is written in a special two-column layout.

fork.setup: you're Moses, about to die, and you need witnesses who will outlast everyone in the camp. who do you call?
fork.reveal: 'give ear, ye heavens... let the earth hear': witnesses that last, and that answer with rain and crops.

original.note: Hebrew: give ear, listen. the first word of Deuteronomy 32 and the name of the portion.

trapdoor: what it means: the sky and the ground are called as witnesses because they last and they respond.
what a scholar hears: the Sifrei contrasts Moses' 'give ear, heavens' with Isaiah 1:2's reversed order; the song is laid out in two columns in the scroll.

sources.quoted: Give ear, ye heavens, and I will speak; And let the earth hear the words of my mouth.

notes: Deuteronomy 32:1 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify capitalization of poetic lines.
Rashi on 32:1 (witnesses that endure; heaven gives rain, earth gives produce) paraphrased.

Sifrei 306: Moses near heaven says 'give ear' (ha'azinu) to heaven; Isaiah near earth reverses. The script glosses ha'azinu as 'listening up close' and shim'u as 'from further off' following the Sifrei's logic; Keeper may refine.
Ha'azinu is written in two columns (Talmud, Shabbat 103b; Soferim). Verify phrasing.
Editor review (y2 520–537): 'Moses' last long words' corrected (the blessings of chapter 33 follow); 'whole history' softened.
